Antiochene School
an-tee-OK-een skool
noun phrase (a school of exegesis)
From Antioch in Syria; the early Christian school of biblical interpretation marked by literal, historical, and grammatical exegesis, in contrast to the allegorical method of Alexandria.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Antiochene school was the early Christian tradition of biblical interpretation centred at Antioch in Syria—the city where the disciples were first called Christians—distinguished by its attention to the literal, historical, and grammatical sense of Scripture, in contrast to the allegorical method that prevailed at Alexandria. Where the Alexandrians, following Origen, sought hidden spiritual meanings beneath the plain words and often dissolved the history into symbol, the Antiochenes insisted on the historia, the real events and the author's intended sense, reading prophecy and type in their grounding in genuine history. The dictionary commends the Antiochene instinct as broadly sound and akin to the historical-grammatical method the Reformers recovered: Scripture has one true sense, to be drawn out by attention to its words, grammar, and historical setting, and read as the apostles read it, with Christ as its scope. The greatest fruit of the school was John Chrysostom, the “golden-mouthed” preacher whose expository sermons through whole books of the Bible remain a model of careful, text-driven preaching. Yet the dictionary does not idealize the school. Its method, pressed without the safeguards of the rule of faith, contributed in some hands to error: Theodore of Mopsuestia and especially Nestorius, products of the Antiochene tradition, so divided the natures of Christ as to fall into the Nestorian heresy condemned at Ephesus. The dictionary therefore commends the literal-historical method as the right foundation, while insisting it be governed by the analogy of faith and the catholic creeds, lest a true principle of interpretation be turned, by neglect of the whole counsel of God, into a doorway for heresy.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The early Christian school of interpretation at Antioch, marked by literal, historical, and grammatical exegesis against Alexandrian allegory; sound in method (its fruit Chrysostom), yet in some hands (Nestorius) leading to Christological error.

ANTIOCHENE SCHOOL, noun phrase. The early Christian school of biblical interpretation centred at Antioch in Syria.

Marked by literal, historical, and grammatical exegesis, against Alexandrian allegory.

Akin to the historical-grammatical method the Reformers recovered.

Its greatest fruit was John Chrysostom, the model expository preacher.

Pressed without safeguards, it bred error in Theodore of Mopsuestia and Nestorius.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Ti 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

Ne 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

2 Pe 1:20 — "Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation."

Ac 11:26 — "And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Alexandrian allegory the Antiochenes opposed dissolved the historical sense into symbol; yet the Antiochene method, unguarded by the rule of faith, bred the Nestorian division of Christ's natures.

expand to see more

The chief error the Antiochene school rightly resisted was the runaway allegory of Alexandria, which, following Origen, sought hidden spiritual meanings beneath the plain text and often treated the history as mere husk to be discarded for the kernel of symbol. The dictionary sides with the Antiochene instinct, and with the Reformers who recovered it: Scripture has one true sense, grounded in real history and the author's intent, to be drawn out by grammar and context and read with Christ as its scope. Allegory unmoored from the literal sense becomes a tool by which any meaning may be imposed on any text.

Yet the dictionary marks the opposite danger that grew within the Antiochene tradition itself. A method that rightly honours the distinct historical realities can, pressed without the governing rule of faith and the catholic creeds, over-divide; and so Theodore of Mopsuestia and especially Nestorius so separated the two natures of Christ as to teach two persons, the heresy condemned at Ephesus in 431. The dictionary's conclusion is balanced: the literal, historical, grammatical method is the sound foundation of all faithful interpretation, but it must be governed by the analogy of faith and the orthodox confession of Christ, lest a true principle become, by neglect of the whole counsel of God, a doorway to error.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Antioch in Syria, the missionary church where believers were first called Christians; its method prized the historia (the historical sense) and the grammatical reading of the text.

expand to see more

Antiocheia, the Syrian city where disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26).

Historia, Greek, the historical sense the school prized over allegory.

Theoria, the Antiochene term for legitimate spiritual sense grounded in the literal.

Set against the Alexandrian allegorical method of Origen and his successors.

Its method anticipates the Reformers' historical-grammatical exegesis.

Usage

"The teacher commended the Antiochene school's literal method as akin to the Reformers' exegesis."

"He noted that Chrysostom's expository preaching was the school's finest fruit."

"She warned that even a sound method, ungoverned by the rule of faith, led Nestorius into error."
